04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The newspaper archivist's reply was useful chiefly because it narrowed what Emma could legitimately claim. Staff had checked the October 2011 subject-index entry headed “Student Travel — decision not received”, but access to the original correspondence remained restricted. The archivist could confirm its index date—12 October—and explained that newspaper employees had written the heading. It was not necessarily a quotation from the person who submitted the letter.

Emma realised how easily she had nearly mistaken an archive label for a witness statement. She forwarded the clarification to Sarah, who called immediately.

“Doesn't the heading still suggest somebody was waiting for a decision?”

“It suggests the archive classified a letter that way. We haven't seen its wording, and we don't know whether the writer was an applicant, a parent or someone else.”

The date placed the indexed item after Claire's disappearance, but Emma had no basis for linking the two events. Chronological proximity did not establish a connection.

Fiona Bell supplied a separate update from the trust. The records team had not identified a verified register of returned decision notices. They had located an unused “Contact attempt” form with fields for a reference number, a date and the action taken. Fiona stressed that no completed example had yet been found.

The form fitted the office manual's instructions for dealing with returned post. Even together, however, the two documents described a possible administrative process rather than proving that staff followed it. Emma recorded the distinction beside her notes on the dispatch ledger.

Sarah suggested trying to identify the October letter's author. Emma was reluctant to turn an archival question into a search for a private individual's identity. She asked the archivist a narrower question instead: could staff establish how many entries concerning the student travel scheme appeared in the surviving index, without releasing correspondence or names? The archivist agreed to investigate but warned that any count might be incomplete.

Emma returned to the procedure governing reviews. Students were supposed to request reconsideration within fourteen days of receiving their decision. A dispatch date did not establish receipt, and the blank contact form could not show what happened when delivery was uncertain.

“Then the deadline might have been impossible to use,” Sarah said.

“Might have been,” Emma replied. “We still lack a real case and any evidence about how the trust applied the rule.”

She drew a careful distinction in her notebook between a weakness that could exist in a system and a failure shown to have occurred. The former justified questions. Only evidence of the latter could support a factual allegation.

By evening, two institutions had promised to check their records. Neither had confirmed a missed notification or an unfair refusal of appeal. Emma ended the day not with a revelation, but with a sharper test: what would have counted as proof that an applicant had received the decision from which the fourteen days ran?
